paper_title: Intrinsic Goals for Autonomous Agents: Hierarchical Exploration Captures Future Volitional Action in Drosophila

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Animals have a remarkable capacity for autonomy---driven by intrinsic motivation---without external sensory cues or extrinsic objectives, yet the computational mechanisms behind this ability largely remain a mystery. We combine whole-brain recordings in the fruit fly (Drosophila melanogaster), which reveal neural representations of spontaneous exploratory decisions more than 10 seconds in advance, with a neuromechanical digital twin to test whether optimizing intrinsic goals yields realistically embodied artificial agents that quantitatively match fly behavior and internal representations of future volitional action during exploration. Our hierarchical policy selects from a discrete library of low-level motor primitives, consistent with ethological theories of behavioral syllables. We train agents without external reward using 20 intrinsic motivation algorithms spanning curiosity, entropy, and competency methods. The agents are evaluated in a virtual tethered-ball assay modeled on the fly experiment, comparing spontaneous locomotor statistics and internal representations and decoding future turn direction from kinematics and neural activity on the same timescales observed in flies. DIAYN, a hierarchical competency algorithm learning discrete policies that maximize behavioral entropy and the separability of induced sensory observations, achieves the strongest joint behavioral and neural prospective coding performance relative to flies. Its learned policies closely capture individual variability in fly exploration strategies, suggesting that this diversity serves to maximize state-space coverage at the population level. DIAYN's latent activity also closely captures the sum-difference rule for interhemispheric encoding of kinematics in biological flies. These results establish hierarchical, intrinsically motivated agents as a powerful framework for reverse-engineering animal autonomy.

sections.title: ABSTRACT
sections.content: Animals have remarkable ability to act autonomouslydriven by intrinsic motivationwithout external sensory cues or extrinsic objectives, yet the computational mechanisms behind this ability largely remain mystery. To understand how biological autonomy may emerge from optimizing intrinsic goals, we use recent whole-brain recordings in the fruit fly (Drosophila melanogaster) that identify neural representations of spontaneous exploratory decisions more than 10 seconds in advance. Combined with neuromechanical digital twin of Drosophila, these recordings allow us to test whether intrinsically motivated artificial agents with realistic embodiments quantitatively match fly behavior and internal representations of future volitional action during exploration. We implement hierarchical, intrinsically motivated agent whose policy operates over discrete library of motor primitivesfixed low-level controllers that actuate joint dynamics closely matching ethological theories of behavioral syllables. We train agents with no external reward using 20 intrinsic motivation algorithms spanning curiosity, entropy, and competency methods. We evaluate frozen policies in virtual tethered-ball assay modeled after the fruit-fly experiment, allowing us to compare spontaneous locomotor statistics and internal representations and decode future turn direction from both kinematics and neural activations on the same timescales observed in flies. We find that DIAYNa hierarchical competency algorithm that learns discrete set of policies maximizing behavioral entropy and the separability of their induced sensory observationsachieves the strongest joint behavioral and neural prospective coding performance with the fruit fly. Surprisingly, DIAYNs learned policies closely capture individual variability in fly exploration strategies, suggesting that this behavioral diversity optimizes concrete computational goal of maximizing state-space coverage at the population level. Furthermore, DIAYN agents latent activity closely captures the specific sum-difference rule in interhemispheric encoding of future kinematics in biological flies. Together, these results establish hierarchical, intrinsically motivated agents as powerful framework for reverse-engineering animal autonomy.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Animals continuously structure experience even in the absence of an explicit task, external reward, or instructive sensory cue. They explore their environment and learn about how their own actions affect the world before those experiences are necessarily tied to particular extrinsic goal. Such selfdirected experience may contribute to the flexibility with which animals later learn new tasks, adapt to changing environments, and acquire new behaviors over their lifetime. In contrast, artificial agents are commonly optimized for extrinsic objectives and task-specific reward functions, and achieving Equal contribution. The angular and forward velocities are read from the ball, analogous to the biological experiment of Brezovec et al. (2023). (c) The policy receives olfaction as weighted sum of intensities sampled at the antennae and maxillary palps. (d) The policys proprioceptive input comes directly from NeuroMechFly and includes joint angles, joint velocities, and body-frame gravity, height, and linear and angular velocities. Understanding the computational objectives that explain intrinsically-driven animal behavior may therefore provide principles for building artificial agents that autonomously learn useful representations and behaviors without extrinsic goals (Keller et al., 2025). wide range of intrinsic-motivation objectives have been proposed as computational mechanisms for generating autonomous behavior in the context of exploration and reinforcement learning. These include objectives such as novelty (Burda et al., 2019), prediction error (Pathak et al., 2017), uncertainty (Pathak et al., 2019), state-space coverage (Liu & Abbeel, 2021), empowerment (Klyubin et al., 2008), and unsupervised skill discovery (Eysenbach et al., 2019). However, these methods are typically evaluated according to criteria designed for artificial agents, such as downstream task performance on highly specific environments. Such evaluations do not directly test for autonomy, nor do they establish whether the resulting behavior or internal representations resemble those of biological agentssystems that already exhibit robust autonomous behavior. Biological systems therefore provide an additional and independently motivated constraint on the space of possible intrinsic objectives. Hence, candidate objective should not only produce useful exploration, but ideally reproduce measurable properties of animal behavior and neural activity (Keller et al., 2025). Recent whole-brain recordings in Drosophila provide particularly useful ground-truth target for these kinds of comparisons. Brezovec et al. (2023) recorded neural activity while head-fixed flies explored spontaneously on spherical treadmill in darkness. They found that interhemispheric activity in subregion of the Inferior Posterior Slope (IPS) was weakly but significantly predictive of future left-versus-right turn direction approximately 15 to 8 seconds before turn. This activity emerged well before the onset of widespread locomotion-related activity across the brain. This provides two complementary constraints on computational hypotheses of internally generated behavior; namely, the spatial and temporal dynamics of the agents behavior and internal representations of future actions. Methods in computational ethology that describe spontaneous behavior of recurring behavioral syllables (Wiltschko et al., 2015; Mathis et al., 2018; Hsu & Yttri, 2021; Pereira et al., 2022) motivate us to consider the level of behavioral abstraction at which the intrinsic-drive methods should operate. 2 Preprint. Under Review. These syllables exhibit organizational structure across multiple timescales, motivating our implementation of hierarchical policy distribution over motor primitives. These motor primitives are then implemented at the joint-torque level by low-level central pattern generator (CPG) (Mantziaris et al., 2020; Chun et al., 2021; Lobato-Rios et al., 2022) and kinematic replays of real fly behaviors, such as grooming (Fig. 2b). This separates exploratory action selection from the mechanics of locomotion and allows intrinsic objectives to operate over behaviorally meaningful variables rather than individual motor commands. We extend the goal-driven modeling approach of computational neuroscience (Yamins & DiCarlo, 2016; Richards et al., 2019; Feather et al., 2025), in which candidate objectives are instantiated in artificial networks and compared against neural recordings, to intrinsic motivation (Keller et al., 2025). We require that candidate objective account for behavior as well as neural activity. Our agents are embodied in NeuroMechFly v2, biomechanical model of Drosophila simulated in FlyGym, with vision, olfaction, proprioception, and articulated body dynamics (Lobato-Rios et al., 2022; Wang-Chen et al., 2024)  (Fig. 1)  . We train recurrent policies with 20 intrinsic drive methods (IDM) spanning curiosity, entropy, and competency objectives (Fig. 2a). All methods share the same embodiment, architecture, training environment, and training budget. We then freeze each policy and evaluate it in virtual tethered-ball assay that reproduces the biological experiment of Brezovec et al. (2023) (Fig. 1b). For each agent, we compare turning behavior with that of the flies, test whether internal representations predict future turn direction on the timescale of the IPS signal, compare this with what ongoing behavior alone predicts, ask whether its low-dimensional activity shares IPSs sum-difference relationship to angular and forward velocity. Contributions To summarize, our contributions are as follows: We implement hierarchical, intrinsically motivated agents embodied in biomechanically-realistic fly body, in which 20 intrinsic objectives operate over seven ethologically motivated behavioral primitives. We show that representations of future action can emerge from intrinsic motivation alone, without an externally specified task or reward. In particular, several intrinsically motivated agents develop internal states that predict turn direction seconds in advance, paralleling the prospective signal observed in the fly IPS. Among the intrinsic objectives tested, unsupervised skill discovery provides the strongest computational account of spontaneous population-wide fly behavior and its neural dynamics. DIAYN, hierarchically operating on behavioral primitives, jointly reproduces future-action predictivity, the relationship between neural and behavioral predictability, inter-animal variability in turning behavior, and low-dimensional activity structure related to forward and angular velocity. We demonstrate that behavioral predictability and average locomotor statistics alone are insufficient to distinguish candidate explanations of spontaneous action. Objectives that generate predictable behavior or match mean turning bias can fail to reproduce the flys prospective internal signal; jointly evaluating behavioral variability and internal future-action predictivity distinguishes DIAYN from these alternatives.

sections.title: 2 BACKGROUND AND RELATED WORK
sections.content: 2.1 INTRINSICALLY GENERATED AND HIERARCHICALLY STRUCTURED ANIMAL BEHAVIOR Animals generate spontaneous behavior in the absence of explicit external reward or immediate instructive cues. Such cases provide valuable setting for studying internally generated action selection. The field of computational ethology has shown that the behavior of animals such as the fly (Berman et al., 2014; 2016; Katsov et al., 2017), mouse (Wiltschko et al., 2015), zebrafish (Marques et al., 2018) and C. elegans (Kaplan et al., 2020) can be decomposed into behavioral syllables (Anderson & Perona, 2014). behavioral syllable is simply recurring, stereotyped pattern of movement that can be reused and combined with other syllables to form more complex behavior. Recent studies have shown behavior exhibits hierarchical organization across syllables and across timescales. Specifically, across species, animal behavior can be represented at multiple nested levels of abstraction, with fine grained behavioral states carrying predictive information over short 3 Preprint. Under Review. timescales and coarser groupings being informative over longer timescales (Berman et al., 2016; Kaplan et al., 2020; Mathis et al., 2018; Hsu & Yttri, 2021; Pereira et al., 2022). Advances in whole-brain neuroimaging of awake and behaving animals has provided unprecendented access to the neural dynamics of complex behavior (Mu et al., 2019; Mann et al., 2021; Aimon et al., 2023; Brezovec et al., 2024a). For example, Mu et al. (2019) image over 200,000 cells spanning neurons and astrocytes in autonomously behaving larval zebrafish, finding that glial cells play crucial role in behavior by accumulating sensorimotor prediction error signaled by neurons. Here, we utilize recordings in flies during autonomous behavior by Brezovec et al. (2023) showing that across bilaterally matched, locomotion-related superclusters distributed around the brain, summed bilateral activity was highly correlated with forward velocity, whereas interhemispheric activity differences were highly correlated with angular velocity. Crucially, this asymmetry emerges much earlier in subregion of the IPS than the rest of the brain, around 15 to 8 seconds before turn. Using this regions activity, future turn direction can be predicted above chance. These findings provide measurable behavioral and representational signatures of internally generated action against which computational models can be evaluated. The multiscale organization of animal behavior motivates us to test hierarchical architecture in which intrinsic drive operates over higher-level locomotor primitives while fixed low-level controllers execute joint dynamics. 2.2 COMPUTATIONAL THEORIES OF INTRINSIC MOTIVATION While the complete tapestry of intrinsic motivations that drive autonomous behavior in animals is not yet understood, multiple computational theories have been proposed to capture some essential qualities of exploration. We organize the methods by the primary quantity they reward into three broad families: curiosity (latent prediction-error), entropy (replay diversity), and competency (policy identifiability). This taxonomy is intended as an organizational device rather than strict partition of mutually exclusive principles. Curiosity Animals are driven by desire to understand their environment and their place within it. This can be described as information-seeking behavior, which can be formalized in variety of ways (Kidd & Hayden, 2015). Most intuitively, an animal can learn forward model of sensory or sensorimotor dynamics and use its prediction-error or uncertainty over time to quantify how In reinforcemuch it understands things and makes progress thereafter (Schmidhuber, 2009). ment learning, this idea was taken seriously and developed early on by Schmidhuber (Schmidhuber, 1991a;b; 1997; 1999), leading to the development of numerous variants and adaptations. In this paper, we choose representative mix of curiosity methods, from prediction-error to informationgain to learning progress. This includes Disagreement (Pathak et al., 2019), γ-Progress (Kim et al., 2020), Intrinsic Curiosity Module (ICM) (Pathak et al., 2017), Model-based Active Exploration (MAX) (Shyam et al., 2019), Never Give Up (NGU) (Badia et al., 2020), Random Network Distillation (RND) (Burda et al., 2019), and Curiosity-driven Exploration via Temporal Contrastive Learning (C-TeC) (Mohamed et al., 2026). The essential object in all algorithms is some predictive model, and they differ in what exactly is predicted or how that model is used to form the intrinsic reward. Entropy Not all kinds of exploration are best explained by drive to understand or predict the world. On the contrary, pursuing sensory novelty for noveltys sake means that one might not care why or how stimulus was produced. For example, mice enjoy highly variable sensory stimuli independently of learning. This preference persists, and even increases, after familiarity with the stimulus contingencies (Olsen & Winder, 2012; Dickson & Mittleman, 2020), suggesting animals are driven by the overall entropy of experience. Thus, entropy-based methods reward novelty with respect to the state or feature distribution, encouraging broad exploration coverage independent of preditability under an internal model. This family includes Active Pretraining (APT) (Liu & Abbeel, 2021), Reinforcement Learning with Prototypical Representations (Proto-RL) (Yarats et al., 2021), and State Entropy Maximization with Random Encoders for Efficient Exploration (RE3) (Seo et al., 2021). Competency Animals often behave to specifically isolate the role of their actions in generating sensory observations, akin to learning causal model of the world in which controllability plays central role. This was coined as Empowerment and formalized by (Klyubin et al., 2008) as the channel capacity between actions and sensory states, encouraging the agent to occupy states in which its actions have influence on future states (Mohamed & Rezende, 2015; Zhao et al., 2021). We consider some additional variants, such as Empowerment Progress (Becker-Ehmck et al., 2021) and Process Empowerment (Tiomkin et al., 2025), which track the channel capacity over time or maximize the capacity under the policy distribution, respectively. We evaluate forward, gain, potential, and process variants of empowerment. Skill-discovery (or options-discovery) methods apply the idea of empowerment to entire policies rather than individual actions by introducing hierarchical skill variable that indexes different policies. Then, mutual information is maximized between each skill and the states induced under that skill. This family includes Contrastive Successor Features (CSF) (Zheng et al., 2025), Dynamics-Aware Unsupervised Discovery of Skills (DADS) (Sharma et al., 2020), Diversity is All You Need (DIAYN) (Eysenbach et al., 2019), Variational Autoencoding Learning of Options by Reinforcement (VALOR) (Achiam et al., 2018), and Variational Intrinsic Control (VIC) (Gregor et al., 2017). 2.3 ARTIFICIAL NEURAL NETWORKS AS HYPOTHESES OF BIOLOGICAL COMPUTATION major approach in computational neuroscience and NeuroAI is to treat task-optimized artificial neural networks as candidate models of biological computation (Yamins & DiCarlo, 2016; Richards et al., 2019). Representations learned by ANNs have been compared to single brain areas, such as the primate visual cortex (Yamins et al., 2013; Khaligh-Razavi & Kriegeskorte, 2014; Cadena et al., 2019), mouse visual cortex (Bakhtiari et al., 2021; Nayebi et al., 2023), the rodent entorhinal system (Banino et al., 2018; Nayebi et al., 2021), auditory cortex (Kell et al., 2018; Feather et al., 2019) and the motor system (Sussillo et al., 2015; Michaels et al., 2020). More recently, NeuroAI has leveraged embodied AI to bridge computational neuroscience with behavior, including virtual animal models such as the rodent (Merel et al., 2019; Aldarondo et al., 2024), the fruit fly (Vaxenburg et al., 2025; Lobato-Rios et al., 2022; Wang-Chen et al., 2024), and the zebrafish (Keller et al., 2025). sections.title: 3 METHODS
sections.content: 3.1 HIERARCHICAL AGENT ARCHITECTURE AND BIOMECHANICAL MODEL Our agents are embodied in NeuroMechFly v2, neuromechanical digital twin of an adult female Drosophila simulated in FlyGym with MuJoCo at timestep of 104 seconds (Lobato-Rios et al., 2022; Wang-Chen et al., 2024; Wang-Chen & Ramdya, 2026; Todorov et al., 2012). The policy receives compound-eye vision from paleand yellow-type ommatidia, bilateral olfactory signal, and proprioceptive state of joint angles, joint velocities, and body kinematics (Fig. 1ce; App. A.1). Control is divided hierarchically  (Fig. 2)  . Every 100 ms, the policy selects one of seven behavioral primitives: forward, left, hard left, right, hard right, stop, and groom. The six locomotor primitives set left and right descending signals that modulate central pattern generator (CPG), whose phase indexes step trajectories recorded from real walking flies (Mantziaris et al., 2020; Chun et al., 2021). The groom primitive executes kinematic replay of recorded fly grooming (App. A.2). Behavior therefore arises from the policy chaining primitives across many decisions, while joint-level mechanics are fixed across all intrinsic objectives. Modality-specific encoders produce 310-dimensional feature vector that feeds separate actor and critic LSTMs (256 units each), followed by MLP heads. The actor outputs categorical distribution over the seven primitives (Fig. 2a; Table 2). For skillconditioned methods, the skill vector is appended to the input of both LSTMs but withheld from the intrinsic reward module. 6 Preprint. Under Review. Figure 4: Turning Bias. (a) Distribution of turning bias across evaluation rollouts for each method. Points indicate individual rollouts, with the mean and range shown for each method. DIAYN produces broad distribution of turning biases spanning more of the fly-to-fly variability than the other evaluated methods. Methods with rollout containing no turns or turns in only one direction are excluded because log(NR/NL) is undefined for those rollouts. (b) Virtual x-y trajectories integrated from the ball state of the nine flies and the nine DIAYN evaluation skills drawn from common origin. 3. INTRINSIC DRIVE METHODS AND TRAINING We train 20 intrinsically motivated policies using methods across three broad families: curiosity, entropy, and competency (Sec. 2.2; App. A.4). The intrinsic reward is the only learning signal the policy receives. We use Recurrent PPO (Raffin et al., 2021; Schulman et al., 2017) in 2,048 parallel environments, procedurally generated arenas with three odor sources and 12 to 50 obstacles which vary the visual, olfactory, and proprioceptive input per episode (Fig. 1a). All methods share the same architecture, environment, hyperparameters, and budget of 50 million policy decisions  (Table 5)  , and all analyses evaluate the final checkpoint. As controls, we evaluate randomly initialized policies with the same architectures as well as policy trained on an extrinsic odor navigation task (App. A.7). Because DIAYN provides the strongest joint account of the behavioral and neural signatures examined below, we describe its objective here to clarify how skill discovery interacts with our hierarchical motor architecture; implementation details for DIAYN and all other intrinsic-drive methods are provided in App. A.4. DIAYN and Hierarchical Skill Discovery DIAYN (Eysenbach et al., 2019) learns skillconditioned policy by maximizing the objective r(θ) = I(S; Z) + H(A S, Z) = H(Z) H(Z S) + H(A S, Z), (1) where denotes the latent skill (drawn from uniform categorical distribution), ϕ the agent sensory-state  (Fig. 2)  , and the action at time t. In our hierarchical architecture, corresponds to one of the seven behavioral motor primitives rather than joint-level motor command. Here, I(; ) denotes mutual information, H() entropy, and H( ) conditional entropy. The first term, H(Z), encourages diverse skill prior and is constant in our implementation because skills are sampled uniformly. The second term, H(Z S), encourages different skills to induce distinguishable states, such that the skill can be inferred from the states it visits. The final term, H(A S, Z), encourages high-entropy action selection within each skill. Thus, each skill learns distinct strategy for selecting among the same shared set of motor primitives as function of the sensory state. sections.title: 3.3 TETHERED-BALL EVALUATION
sections.content: Frozen policies are evaluated in virtual version of the assay of Brezovec et al. (2023), where the fly is head-fixed on 9 mm air-supported ball, and angular and forward velocity are read from the ball simulator state (Fig. 1b). To match the darkness and absence of odor in the biological experiment, visual and olfactory inputs are set to zero. For each policy we collect nine 30-minute rollouts, matching the nine flies and 270 minutes of biological data. All policies are evaluated via sampling. Skills are sampled once at the start of each episode and resampled whenever the number of decisions reaches the methods skill horizon. The LSTM hidden state is not reset during the evaluation. Details are given in App. A.6.

sections.title: 4 RESULTS
sections.content: Behavioral data is processed identically for agents and flies matching the procedure of Brezovec et al. (2023). First, velocities are smoothed with 500 ms Savitzky-Golay filter (Savitzky & Golay, 1964). Then, turns are detected as peaks in absolute angular velocity above 200/s (Brezovec et al., 2023). Each evaluation rollout or fly experiment is summarized by its turning bias, log(NR/NL). To test for prototypical planning representation, we decode future turn direction from the activity in the 15 to 8 window using elastic-net penalized logistic regression (Zou & Hastie, 2005; Pedregosa et al., 2011) with five-fold stratified cross-validation and report balanced accuracy (Brodersen et al., 2010). Decoder hyperparameters are tuned once on the fly data and fixed for all agents. For agents, we evaluate seven candidate internal representations: the actor LSTM, critic LSTM, policy MLP, and value MLP representations individually, together with three concatenations of these recorded features. The largest concatenation additionally includes the learned observation embedding. As separate input-level control, we also decode from the raw proprioceptive observation, with vision and odor zeroed. For the biological fly, performance is decoded from IPS activity (App. A.8). Because future turns may be predictable from current behavior alone, we fit the same decoder to mean angular and forward velocity in the same window to identify policies that converged to relatively stable, predictable behavioral strategy (App. A.9). Finally, to compare the representation geometry without assuming an anatomical correspondence, we apply PCA to each agents activity in its highest-performing neural layer for decoding. We test whether pairs of components relate to angular and forward velocity as the IPS hemispheres do (App. A.11). Neural and Behavioral Decoding Using the network activations from the models in the tetheredball evaluation, we follow the same conceptual test used for the biological fly, asking whether internal activity before turn predicts its eventual direction and plot the prospective coding in Fig. 3a. The biological fly IPS has neural prospective coding of 66.5 1.4% while DIAYN and NGU of the IDM-trained models approach or exceed this performance with 82.1 0.9% and 65.4 1.8% respectively (Fig. 3a). Many IDM-trained policies are near 50% prospective coding or had an undefined prospective coding due to never having detected turn or only having detected turns of single direction. Neither condition permits stratified fold cross-validation for the accuracy calculation. Analogously, we decode turn direction from behavior. Using the mean angular (ω) and forward (v) velocity of the ball in the before-turn window, we fit logistic regression classifier to decode the future direction of the turn and plot the prospective coding in Fig. 3c. For the flies, behavior alone predicts future turn direction with prospective coding of 60.5 0.9%. For the IDM-trained policies, many exhibit behavior that is predictive of future turn direction and decodable including MAX (92.2 5.9%), DIAYN (74.7 1.4%), γ-progress (72.4 1.2%) and NGU (66.3 9.4%). Nine of the 20 methods produce no turns or turns in only one direction during evaluation (Fig. 3e), itself behavioral mismatch with the fly. Performance Ratio These results distinguish IDMs that produce internally predictive representations from those whose behavior is simply easy to predict from past behavior. Critically, an agent whose behavior resembles the flys should show similar ratio of neural to behavioral decoding accuracy: internal states should carry predictive information beyond behavior, while behavior itself is structured but not trivially predictable. Therefore, Fig. 3d considers neural and behavioral predictability jointly. Among the trained agents, DIAYN and NGU are the only IDMs that match or exceed the neural and behavioral predictability of the fly. Unlike NGU, DIAYN also maintains the same ratio of predictability as the fly. 8 Preprint. Under Review. Figure 5: Low-dimensional internal structures relate to ω and v. Turning Bias Models that match the mean statistics of the flies do not match the flies population variability. Fig. 4a shows each models distribution of turning biases. Models whose mean bias is close to the flies, such as APT and the random controls, do not reproduce the fly population of turning biases. In contrast, DIAYNs skills span much wider range of turning biases, yielding more similar state space coverage to the flies (Fig. 4b) based on trajectory coverage. DIAYN holds one skill per 30-minute rollout, so its nine rollouts sample nine skills, paralleling the nine flies. CSF and Random-DIAYN use the same schedule yet show far narrower bias distributions (Fig. 4a), indicating that the fly-like spread arises from the learned objective rather than the sampling scheme. Internal Representations The internal activation dynamics of the models were also compared with the fly neural dynamics. As shown in Fig. 5a, neural activity in the fly IPS forms separable structures whose difference and sum is correlated with angular and forward velocity, respectively. Fig. 5b shows that trained DIAYN recovers similar relationship, whereas this organization is absent in the random-initialized control (Fig. 5c). For trained DIAYN, the difference of the selected component pair correlates with ω (r = 0.153) and their sum with (r = 0.413), comparable to the fly IPS (r = 0.191 and 0.429). In Random-DIAYN, the best pair reaches only = 0.021 and 0.113.

sections.title: 5 DISCUSSION
sections.content: The central implication of our results is that behavioral diversity and prospective internal activity may reflect shared computational objective. Methods that match average turning bias or generate highly predictable behavior need not reproduce the accompanying predictive neural representation (Figs. 3 and 4). DIAYNs joint correspondence with these properties therefore motivates an explanation of autonomy that addresses both the diversity of spontaneous behavior and the internal organization that makes future actions predictable. In our hierarchical implementation, DIAYN learns strategies for selecting among seven motor primitives, so its objective concerns the organization of behavior above the level of individual motor commands. It rewards skills that induce distinguishable sensory states while encouraging highentropy action selection within each skill. Because each skill is held fixed throughout training or 9 Preprint. Under Review. evaluation episode, we interpret it as persistent exploratory strategy consistent with the locomotor handedness observed in individual flies (Buchanan et al., 2015; Ayroles et al., 2015; de Bivort et al., 2022). Brezovec et al. (2023) show wide individual variation in fly exploration strategies, as reflected in their turning biases, and remarkably, DIAYNs learned repertoire of skills captures this variation quite well  (Fig. 4)  . The repertoire thus offers model of behavioral diversity across population of flies. One possible explanation is that the fly brains limited computational capacity favors single, relatively fixed exploratory strategy per individual, while the diversity of strategies needed for survival is realized through their distribution across individuals to maximize state-space coverage as population. Under this hypothesis, evolutionary pressures favor diverse individual strategies that collectively maximize coverage of sensory space. Handedness and other persistent behavioral tendencies we observe in individuals could also be interpreted as individual expressions of this population-level diversity. Skill discovery may also help explain why internal activity becomes predictive of future turns. Although DIAYNs intrinsic reward is evaluated at individual time steps, PPO optimizes the policy to maximize cumulative intrinsic reward over trajectories. This optimization can favor sustained patterns of behavior that keep the sensory states induced by different skills distinguishable over time. In our hierarchical controller, such patterns can arise through persistent, skill-dependent tendencies to select particular motor primitives. The recurrent state may therefore encode the ongoing exploratory strategy and carry information about turns that occur seconds later. Under this hypothesis, prospective activity reflects the ongoing organization of behavioral strategy rather than moment-by-momemnt movements, consistent with the findings in real fruit flies in Brezovec et al. (2023). Hierarchical skill-discovery therefore provides concrete computational framework in which animal-like behavioral diversity and future-action representations emerge together under common intrinsic objective.

sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We introduce framework for reverse-engineering animal autonomy that combines neuromechanical digital twin, hierarchical control over behavioral primitives, and joint comparison with fly behavior and neural recordings. Across 20 intrinsic objectives, DIAYN provides the strongest account of individual differences in turn decisions, prospective neural activity, and interhemispheric sumdifference encoding of kinematics. Importantly, these properties emerge entirely from optimizing self-supervised, intrinsic goal without training on external rewards or fly data. Our results show that individual behavioral variability and shared representations of future action can arise from the same computational objective. DIAYN links these findings through persistent exploration strategies whose internal states predict future turns seconds in advance. This suggests novel perspective on the role of individual differences in optimizing exploration at the population level, an efficient strategy for survival of species when the capacity of individual members is limited. These results establish the importance of using both neural and behavioral data in distinguishing computational models, the role of hierarchy in designing agents that naturally express complex behavior, and the potential of embodied agents and intrinsic reinforcement learning to understand principles of animal autonomy. LIMITATIONS AND FUTURE WORK One main limitation of our approach is the choice to constrain the space of behaviors available to each policy to the predefined locomotor primitives and low-level controllers. While this reflects the hierarchical organization of animal behavior, it limits the learned behavior primarily to 2-D locomotion. Future work could learn the primitives jointly with their high-level selection, allowing the IDM to shape its low-level repertoire, or expanding the primitives to allow flight, potentially extending the pre-existing implementation of Vaxenburg et al. (2025). Another opportunity is to extend our framework to account for the whole-brain dynamics of locomotion (Brezovec et al., 2024a). Due to our focus on IPS, simple training environment was sufficient to reproduce key features of those neural responses. whole-brain pursuit would force us to confront an ethnologically relevant environment with variable terrain, opportunities for manipulation and resources that may favor different intrinsic objectives and thereby generate broader repertoire of behaviorswhich is possible to explore within the agent-based framework we build here. 10 Preprint. The proprioceptive observation is oprop = [q, q, h, gbody, vbody, ωbody] R100, (2) where q, R45 are the angles (rad) and angular velocities (rad/s) of the 45 position-actuated degrees of freedom, is the height of the body root (mm), gbody R3 is gravity in the body frame, and vbody, ωbody R3 are the linear (mm/s) and angular (rad/s) velocities of the body root. The 45 degrees of freedom are seven per leg (thoraxcoxa yaw, pitch, and roll; coxatrochanter pitch and roll; femurtibia pitch; tibiatarsus pitch), ordered LF, LM, LH, RF, RM, RH, followed by neck pitch, roll, and yaw (Fig. 1d). Vision. Each compound eye is rendered by fisheye camera (512 450 pixels, 157 field of view) and read out as 721 ommatidia, 505 yellow-type and 216 pale-type (Lobato-Rios et al., 2022; Wang-Chen et al., 2024). Each ommatidium takes the mean of the green (yellow-type) or blue (paletype) channel over its pixels, scaled to [0, 1]. For computational efficiency, the ommatidial map is resampled from 512 450 to 32 32 grid by nearest-neighbor sampling at each grid-pixel center; grid pixels outside the lattice are zero, and 623 of the 721 ommatidia are represented. The visual input is 2 2 32 32 tensor (eye ommatidium type height width; Fig. 1e). Olfaction. Odor intensity at position is I(x) = (cid:80) Akxxk2, summed over sources with peak amplitude Ak = 1. Intensity is sampled at the left and right maxillary palps and antennae and combined on each side as 0.1 Ipalp + 0.9 Iantenna, giving two-dimensional left/right observation (Fig. 1c). Normalization. Odor and proprioceptive observations are normalized with running means and variances and clipped at 10. Visual input is not normalized. Locomotor primitives drive six-oscillator CPG, GPU reimplementation of the FlyGym hybrid turning controller (Lobato-Rios et al., 2022; Wang-Chen et al., 2024) without its stumbling and retraction correction rules. The groom primitive replays 35-frame (0.35 s) clip of recorded, optogenetically evoked grooming bout (aJO-GAL4 > CsChrimson) at 100 Hz, driving 17 degrees of freedom: the three neck joints and the seven joints of each front leg ( Ozdil et al., 2026). The CPG receives stop signal, the middle and hind legs are held at their pose at groom onset with adhesion on for stability, and the body root is held fixed for the duration of the bout. To avoid abrupt movement, the replay blends in linearly from the onset pose over 0.05 s; on the next non-groom action, control switches back to the CPG. Grooming is not macro-action: each groom action lasts one 0.1 decision, consecutive groom actions continue the clip (looping every 35 frames). A.3 POLICY ARCHITECTURE Policies use the recurrent actorcritic of sb3-contrib RecurrentPPO (Raffin et al., 2021), with shared multimodal feature extractor and separate actor and critic LSTMs (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997) (Fig. 2a; Table 2). CNN (Fukushima, 1980; LeCun et al., 1998) with weights shared across the two eyes produces 64-dimensional embedding per eye, for 128-dimensional visual representation. MLPs (Rumelhart et al., 1986) embed odor (16 dimensions) and proprioception (64 dimensions). The odor embedding is concatenated with the raw 2-dimensional odor observation and the proprioceptive embedding with the raw 100-dimensional proprioceptive state, yielding modality representations of 128, 18, and 164 dimensions and 310-dimensional base feature vector ϕt. This is passed to the actor and critic LSTMs (256 hidden units each) and to the intrinsic drive module (IDM). Separate actor and critic MLP heads follow the LSTMs, and the actor outputs categorical distribution over the seven primitives. For skill-conditioned methods, the skill is appended to ϕt at the input of both LSTMs. The IDM receives only ϕt, never z, which prevents the skill discriminator from being solved trivially. Linear 2; 0.01 for the action head and 1 for and convolutional layers use orthogonal initialization (gain the value head), and the LSTMs use PyTorchs default initialization. We train each policy in procedurally randomized FlyGym environment (Fig. 1a) that exposes the agent to variation in its visual, olfactory, and proprioceptive inputs. Each arena contains three odor sources and 12 to 50 obstacles, regenerated at every episode. Optimization. Policies are trained with Recurrent PPO (Raffin et al., 2021; Schulman et al., 2017) in 2, 048 parallel environments, each with distinct random seed, using the settings in Table 5 and generalized advantage estimation (Schulman et al., 2016). Each method is trained for the same budget of 50 million policy decisions, summed across environments (5 106 of simulated experience, approximately 244 PPO updates). The scalar reward used by PPO is supplied entirely by the intrinsic drive module, so differences between trained policies arise from the intrinsic objective rather than from external task reward. LSTM states are reset at episode starts and carried across rollout boundaries; backpropagation through time runs over sequences split at episode boundaries (at most 50 decisions). Truncated episodes are bootstrapped with the value of the final observation, and optimization epochs stop early when the approximate KL divergence exceeds 1.5 times the target. Each method is trained once, with seed 0. We evaluate the checkpoint at the end of the training budget, without selecting checkpoints on any evaluation metric. Compute and software. Each run used one GPU (NVIDIA L40S or comparable) and 64 CPU cores. Throughput ranged from roughly 80-129 policy decisions per second depending on the method. Recorded training wall time was 108-175 hours per method  (Table 4)  . These times exclude setup, the final PPO update, interrupted work without rollout log, and time between jobs, so they are lower bounds on full job time. Software: Python 3.12, FlyGym 2.1.0, MuJoCo 3.9.0 with MuJoCo-Warp 3.9.0.1, Warp 1.14.0, Stable-Baselines3 and sb3-contrib 2.8.0, PyTorch, and JAX 0.4.33. Turns are local maxima of ω exceeding 200/s, following Brezovec et al. (2023); the turn time is the time of the peak. For flies, peaks in the first and last 40 of each session are discarded. To compare behavior, we compute the number of left and right turns, NL and NR, for each rollout or fly, and the turning bias log(NR/NL). Turning bias is reported only when NL > 0 and NR > 0; otherwise it is undefined, and such rollouts are omitted from bias summaries but retained in turn counts. A.10 DECODING Features. For each turn, features are averaged over window relative to the turn: 15 to 8 (before the turn) or 0.4 to +0.4 (during the turn). For agents, the average is over the 0.532 activation bins whose left edge falls within the window. We record five internal network representations: the learned observation embedding, the actor LSTM hidden state, the critic LSTM hidden state, the policy MLP hidden representation and the value MLP hidden representation. The network decoding (neural prospective coding) analysis evaluates seven candidate feature sets: the actor LSTM, critic LSTM, policy MLP and value MLP individually, and three concatenations of layers: actor LSTM with policy MLP (ACTOR), critic LSTM with value MLP (CRITIC), and all five recorded internal representations (ALL). The learned observation embedding is included in ALL. As separate inputlevel control, we decode from the raw proprioceptive observations with vision and odor set to zero. For flies, features are the window-averaged activity of every voxel in the left and right IPS, concatenated; unlike Brezovec et al. (2023), we neither restrict the analysis to the pre-motor supercluster nor use the interhemispheric difference. Behavioral features are the window means of angular and forward velocity. Classifier. We use logistic regression with an elastic-net penalty (Zou & Hastie, 2005; Pedregosa et al., 2011) and the saga solver (Defazio et al., 2014). A.11 REPRESENTATIONAL ANALYSIS Because the policy has no anatomical analogue of the flys bilaterally matched superclusters, we cannot reproduce the spatial pairing analysis of Brezovec et al. (2023) directly. Instead, we use PCA to identify low-dimensional axes of model activity and ask whether pairs of components show the same functional relationship to behavior: opposing activity associated with angular velocity and shared activity associated with forward velocity. This is functional comparison of representational geometry, not an anatomical correspondence between model components and fly hemispheres. For DIAYN and Random-DIAYN, we fit 10-component PCA (randomized SVD, seed 0) to the actor LSTM activations pooled across all nine rollouts (9 3,384 samples; units centered but not standardized), and scale each component to unit variance. Angular and forward velocity are interpolated to the activation timestamps. For every unordered pair (i, j) of components, we compute Sij = r(PCi PCj, ω) + r(PCi + PCj, v) , (7) where is the Pearson correlation over all timepoints, and select the maximizing pair, breaking ties by the smaller of the two correlations. The pair is oriented so that the difference increases with angular velocity. The same search is applied to the randomly initialized policy as reference. The selected pairs are PCs 2 and 8 for DIAYN and PCs 5 and 10 for Random-DIAYN  (Fig. 5)  . The biological panel (Fig. 5a) is reconstructed from Fig. 1ef of Brezovec et al. (2023).
